cards.headline: St. Lucie County residents adjust diets as E. coli and cyclospora outbreaks spread
cards.teaser: Health officials confirmed five local cases of cyclospora since May, including two in St. Lucie County and one in Martin County, prompting residents to change what they eat and avoid.
cards.body:
Concerns over contaminated produce linked to E. coli and cyclospora outbreaks are prompting South Florida residents to reconsider their food choices, with some avoiding leafy greens entirely. The outbreaks have affected thousands nationwide and include lettuce connected to Taco Bell locations. Health officials have confirmed local cases stretching from the Palm Beaches to the Treasure Coast, including two cases in St. Lucie County.

 The Florida Department of Health reported five confirmed local cases of cyclospora since May. Two cases were reported in Palm Beach County, two in St. Lucie County, and one in Martin County. The contamination concerns have led families across the region to change their eating habits at restaurants, grocery stores, and fast-food chains.

 Dakota and Brynlee Rhodes, who were visiting Delray Beach with their mother Jenny, said they are trying to stay away from lettuce and stuff like that. Other families are similarly steering clear of leafy greens altogether as reports of contaminated produce continue to spread across the country. The widespread nature of the outbreaks has left many consumers uncertain about which products are safe to purchase and consume.

 Samantha Barone, a dietitian for the bariatric program at Delray Medical Center, offered guidance for consumers looking to maintain healthy diets while avoiding potentially contaminated produce. Barone recommends sticking to melon and things that have a harder skin that you can peel. She advises consumers to focus on produce with protective outer layers and to wash all fruits and vegetables thoroughly before eating them.

 For those seeking alternatives to leafy greens, Barone suggests that beans and nuts are safe options that still provide fiber and protein. She specifically recommends cleaning produce using a mixture of one part distilled white vinegar to three parts water. The outbreaks have highlighted the importance of proper food handling and preparation practices for consumers across South Florida.

cards.headline: E. coli and cyclospora outbreaks hit Treasure Coast, residents avoid lettuce and berries
cards.teaser: Two confirmed cases of cyclospora infections occurred in St. Lucie County and one in Martin County since May, part of nationwide E. coli and cyclospora outbreaks linked to contamin
cards.body:
Two confirmed cases of cyclospora infections occurred in St. Lucie County and one in Martin County since May, part of nationwide E. coli and cyclospora outbreaks linked to contaminated lettuce, according to the Florida Department of Health. Palm Beach County reported two additional cases. Thousands across the United States have been affected by the outbreaks, including lettuce connected to Taco Bell locations.

 Residents across South Florida are changing their diets in response to the health threat. Dakota and Brynlee Rhodes, visiting Delray Beach with their mother Jenny, said they are staying away from lettuce. Jenny Rhodes said she misses salads and berries but prefers being careful.

 George Lorenz said he heard about the outbreak and is avoiding contaminated foods while eating pizza in downtown West Palm Beach on Clematis Street with his father Brian. Hendriette Peckens in Boynton Beach bought two big bags of oranges, bread and apples instead of produce and planned to cook Alaskan salmon for dinner.

 Samantha Barone, a dietitian for the bariatric program at Delray Medical Center, said consumers should focus on produce with protective outer layers like melons, bananas and avocados. She said people should stick to melon and things with harder skin that can be peeled, but emphasized the importance of washing them before cutting and peeling. Barone recommended washing all fruits and vegetables thoroughly before eating them and said beans and nuts are safe alternatives that provide fiber and protein.

 She warned against bagged lettuce and recommended buying whole heads of lettuce and peeling away the outer layers. She also advised avoiding berries, especially raspberries, because they are difficult to clean properly. Brian Lorenz said he is not avoiding anything but is washing all food.

 Barone recommended cleaning produce using a one to three part mixture of distilled white vinegar and water, then soaking, massaging and cleaning off produce before cooking vegetables. The outbreaks stem from contaminated produce that can cause severe stomach illness and intense diarrhea. Barone emphasized that the outbreaks are not an excuse to abandon healthy eating, telling people not to say to heck with fruits and vegetables and hit the donuts. She said consumers still want to remain healthy despite the contamination concerns affecting produce typically considered healthier options.

hero.headline: Family files wrongful death lawsuit after 6-year-old killed in go-kart crash at Urban Air in Port St. Lucie
hero.teaser: The family of Emma Riddle filed a wrongful death lawsuit Monday against Urban Air Trampoline and Adventure Park in Port St. Lucie, where the 6-year-old died in a go-kart crash in December 2025.
hero.body:
Emma Riddle, 6, was fatally injured at Urban Air Trampoline and Adventure Park in Port St. Lucie in December 2025. The child visited the adventure park with her mother and sister, where they rode electric go-karts. Emma was seated with her mom in a double-seat go-kart while her older sister was in a single-rider go-kart. According to Morgan & Morgan injury law firm, the family's attorney, there were multiple alleged safety protocols ignored that allegedly led Emma's go-kart to accelerate to a high speed and crash into the track wall. Emma suffered severe injuries and was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she later died.

The wrongful death lawsuit filed Monday alleges that Urban Air created dangerous conditions that contributed to Emma's death. The family claims the adventure park ignored safety rules and manufacturer guidelines. At 50 inches, Emma was nearly a foot shorter and twelve years younger than the manufacturer's minimum stated recommendations for operating a double-seat go-kart, and yet she was permitted to ride, the lawsuit alleges. Earlier this year, the Florida Department of Agriculture reached a $300,000 settlement agreement with Urban Air Adventure Park following an investigation into the fatal incident.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie to Host Low-Cost Rabies and Microchip Drive-Thru Clinic Aug. 22
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie Animal Control will host a Low-Cost Rabies & Microchip Drive-Thru Clinic next month, giving local pet owners an affordable opportunity to vaccinate and microchip the
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie Animal Control will host a Low-Cost Rabies & Microchip Drive-Thru Clinic next month, giving local pet owners an affordable opportunity to vaccinate and microchip their dogs and cats.

The clinic will take place from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturday, Aug. 22, in the Animal Control parking lot at 1133 SW South Macedo Blvd. The drive-thru format allows residents to remain in their vehicles throughout the process. Vehicles should enter from SW Lakehurst Drive via Bayshore Boulevard.

The event is open only to Port St. Lucie residents, who must provide proof of residency, such as a driver's license or utility bill.

For $20 per pet, participants will receive:

- A one-year rabies vaccination
- A microchip
- A City of Port St. Lucie pet license

Dogs and cats must be at least 4 months old to participate. Dogs must arrive on a leash, while cats must be transported in secure carriers. Animal Control officials noted that all dogs will be muzzled during their appointment to ensure staff safety.

The clinic is limited to 200 pets, and walk-up appointments will not be accepted. Pet owners are required to register in advance.

**Preregistration is required.** You can [preregister for the clinic here](https://forms.cityofpsl.com/AnimalLicensing/RabiesMicrochip/RabiesMicrochipForm).

The event is being held in partnership with Caring Fields Feline Sanctuary, Operation SOS, and the Humane Society of St. Lucie County.

cards.headline: Second arrest made in fatal shooting of Fort Pierce art teacher Andre Leonard Barnes
cards.teaser: Dale A. Mincey, 41, Barnes' nephew, was formally charged with first-degree murder Saturday in connection with the July 7 shooting on the 2700 block of Essex Drive.
cards.body:
The fatal shooting happened July 7 at a residence on the 2700 block of Essex Drive. Deputies responded to the home at around 3:30 p.m. after receiving reports of a person with a gunshot wound. When deputies arrived, they learned a man had shot another man with a rifle.

 Barnes was taken to a local hospital, where he died. Dale A. Mincey, 41, Barnes' nephew, was formally charged with first-degree murder Saturday in connection with Barnes' death.

 Mincey remains in custody at the St. Lucie County Jail and is being held without bond. During questioning, Mincey told detectives he could not recall what happened the day of the shooting and that he didn't have any issues with Barnes and did not know how Barnes died, an arrest affidavit said. However, he admitted to owning two firearms.

 Karen Moye, the victim's sister and mother of the suspect, was also at the home when the shooting occurred. She heard a loud bang while she was in the bathroom and came out to find Mincey and called police, an arrest affidavit said. Moye, who lived in the home with Mincey and Barnes, told detectives immediately after the shooting that the pair did not have a good relationship and that Mincey told her he was expressing fear in the days leading up to the shooting.

 Sheriff Richard Del Toro said Moye knowingly provided false information to investigators and withheld pertinent information related to this homicide investigation. She has been charged with false report to law enforcement and the commission of a capital felony. Barnes worked as an art teacher for the St. Lucie County School District since 2017, serving at West Gate K-8 and Samuel S. Gaines Academy.

cards.headline: Some Villa Del Sol residents return home nearly 2 years after structural damage forced evacuation
cards.teaser: Villa Del Sol residents in St. Lucie County told WPTV they are able to return home after nearly two years of being displaced from their condos following structural damage found in August 2024.
cards.body:
Residents told WPTV they were notified last month they could return to their condos, after an inspection in August 2024 found structural damage in buildings 3, 4, and 5, which were deemed unsafe. Katie Johnson was the first to share to WPTV that residents had been told they could come back. WPTV received emails sent to residents from the Board of Directors telling them they could return.

 WPTV also obtained a letter from engineers sent to St. Lucie County's Building Department requesting they lift occupancy restrictions following their special inspection. Katie Johnson described the work still underway at the property, saying they're still moving the dirt back under the buildings.

 Robert Segedin took WPTV inside his family's home, excited to return but thinking about those who cannot. Eric Johnson is among those not coming back. He was one of the first residents WPTV met at Villa Del Sol and is now living in Georgia.

 Eric Johnson said the financial toll has been severe, explaining the family had to drain out all their savings accounts and all their 401ks just trying to make ends meet while this was going on. He is filing for bankruptcy and filing his condo for foreclosure. Katie Johnson said she is thinking of neighbors like Eric Johnson who cannot return, saying she feels so bad that some were hit harder than others with the situation.

cards.headline: New tuition-free tech school opening in Fort Pierce in August
cards.teaser: SouthTech Treasure Coast will open in Fort Pierce in August, giving middle and high school students the opportunity to earn industry certifications while completing their traditional coursework.
cards.body:
A new tuition-free career and technical charter school is preparing to open in Fort Pierce in August. SouthTech Treasure Coast will give middle and high school students the opportunity to earn industry certifications while completing their traditional coursework. The St. Lucie County School Board approved the charter application for the Fort Pierce campus in April.

 School leaders say they selected the Treasure Coast because of the area's growing demand for skilled workers. The Fort Pierce campus will serve students in grades 6 through 12, with plans to enroll about 460 students in its first year.

 Students will have the opportunity to choose from career academies including medical science, culinary arts, cosmetology, and agriculture technology. Carla Lovett, Executive Director of SouthTech Schools, said all students are working on their academics, but they are also all in one of the career academies where they have the opportunity to earn adult level industry certifications while they are still in high school.

 SouthTech Treasure Coast will host a grand opening celebration on Saturday, July 25, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., giving families and community members a chance to tour the new campus and learn more about the programs being offered. SouthTech Treasure Coast in Fort Pierce is located at 2810 S. US Highway 1 Fort Pierce, FL 34982.

cards.headline: Jealousy over woman sparked double fatal shooting in Port St. Lucie, police say
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police said jealousy over a woman prompted an exchange of gunfire that claimed two lives Sunday morning in the 1300 block of Southeast Rivergreen Circle.
cards.body:
The double fatal shooting occurred at about 3:30 a.m. Sunday in the 1300 block of Southeast Rivergreen Circle. When officers arrived, they found two men with multiple gunshot wounds in the driveways of a residence.

 Both victims, identified as Carl Loubeau, 24, and Juliun Stokes, 22, both from Fort Pierce, were taken to separate local hospitals, where they later died from their injuries. Police said a verbal altercation occurred outside the residence over a key to a home and escalated into an exchange of gunfire between two of the individuals involved.

 Chief Leo Niemczyk said a woman contacted Loubeau, whom she was dating, for a key because she was locked out of her home. When Carl arrived, he found her present with other people, including two males. The motive behind the initial attack was jealousy over the female, Niemczyk said.

 Police said Loubeau was the primary aggressor in the dispute, with Dwayne Walker, 20, discharging his firearm in self-defense. Niemczyk said Loubeau approached Juliun and opened fire on him, apparently mistaking him for Dwayne. Walker was in close proximity and withdrew his lawfully carried firearm and started firing on Carl.

 Police said their current investigation shows that Loubeau fired eight rounds from a 9 mm pistol and one round from a .380 pistol, with Walker firing eight rounds from his .40 caliber pistol. Walker was not injured in the incident. No arrests have been made in the case.

hero.headline: Fellsmere animal sanctuary rebuilds with steel structure after fire killed 11 cats
hero.body:
For the Love of Paws in Fellsmere is rebuilding with more than $100,000 in community donations after a fire on March 9 destroyed the sanctuary and killed 11 cats. Ted Pankiewicz founded the nonprofit sanctuary in 2014 in memory of his late wife, who had always wanted to start a rescue organization. Pankiewicz suffered burns to his arms as he tried to save the animals during the fire.

The sanctuary operates differently than traditional rescues, providing permanent homes for animals rather than adopting them out. "We are a sanctuary, we're not a rescue. When your pets come here, they come here for the rest of their life. We take care of them as our very own," Pankiewicz said. For the Love of Paws also distributes 12,000 to 15,000 pounds of pet food monthly to senior citizens, disabled residents, and veterans struggling to feed their pets, serving some of the Treasure Coast's most vulnerable residents.

The new facility will be constructed entirely of steel and include a security system that alerts the fire department directly when smoke is detected. The building will also have an interior sprinkler system to prevent future tragedies. "The new building is going to be all steel, and we're going to be having a security system put in where the smoke detectors immediately alert the fire department, and there will be a sprinkler system inside too, which I'm sure will piss off the cats, but it's better," Pankiewicz said.

The community response left Pankiewicz struggling to find words to express his gratitude. "The response from the community was just as emotional as the fire was, but in the opposite. The fire made us cry tears of sorrow, and the community made us cry tears of gratitude," Pankiewicz said. The new facility is expected to be a cage-free space with an outdoor catio where cats can roam freely.

cards.headline: Free and reduced-price meal applications open for Indian River County students
cards.teaser: Families in Indian River County can apply for free or reduced-price meals for students starting July 15 for the 2026-2027 school year.
cards.body:
Families in Indian River County can apply for free or reduced-price meals for students starting July 15. Students at six Indian River County schools can receive free meals during the 2026-2027 school year through federal nutrition programs. Other families in the district may still qualify for free or reduced-price meals based on household size and income criteria. Families are encouraged to complete one application per household to determine eligibility.

 To apply, families need their child's Student ID number, their child's full formal name as listed in FOCUS, a valid email address, and internet access or the LINQ Connect mobile app. Families who receive Florida Medicaid benefits need their 10-digit Medicaid case number that begins with the number 1. The case number can be found by logging into a MyACCESS account or looking at the Notice of Eligibility Review letter from the Florida Department of Children and Families.

 Families can visit www.LINQConnect.com to sign in or create an account, search for Indian River County Public Schools in Vero Beach, and add their student using the Student ID and formal name. To start the meal application, families should click School Services at the top menu and select Free and Reduced Meal Application. Families with questions can contact Shawn O'Keefe, the district's nutrition services director, at 772-564-5041 or shawn.okeefe@indianriverschools.org.

cards.headline: Fellsmere animal sanctuary rebuilds with $100,000 in community support after fire killed 11 cats

cards.body:
For the Love of Paws in Fellsmere is rebuilding after a fire on March 9 destroyed the sanctuary and killed 11 cats, leaving founder Ted Pankiewicz with burned arms. The community responded by raising more than $100,000 to help the sanctuary rebuild.

 Pankiewicz founded For the Love of Paws in 2014 in memory of his late wife. "We started this in memory of my wife. Starting a rescue or something like that was always something that she always wanted to do," Pankiewicz said.

 The sanctuary operates differently than a traditional rescue, keeping animals for the rest of their lives rather than adopting them out. "We are a sanctuary, we're not a rescue… when your pets come here, they come here for the rest of their life. We take care of them as our very own," Pankiewicz said. The facility supplies 12 to 15,000 pounds of pet food each month to senior citizens, disabled individuals, and veterans who are struggling to feed their pets.

 The new facility will be built entirely of steel and will include a security system that alerts the fire department directly when smoke is detected, along with an interior sprinkler system. "The new building is going to be all steel… and we're going to be having a security system put in where the smoke detectors immediately alert the fire department, and there will be a sprinkler system inside too… which I'm sure will piss off the cats, but it's better," Pankiewicz said. The new facility is expected to be a cage-free space with an outdoor catio where cats can roam freely.

 The outpouring of support from the community left Pankiewicz deeply moved. "The response from the community was just as emotional as the fire was, but in the opposite… the fire made us cry tears of sorrow, and the community made us cry tears of gratitude," Pankiewicz said. The sanctuary serves some of the Treasure Coast's most vulnerable residents and their pets, and the community rallied to ensure it could continue its mission after the devastating fire.

cards.headline: Waterspouts, lightning strikes and fires batter Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County
cards.teaser: Friday's severe weather left a trail of impacts across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County, including waterspouts in Sebastian, lightning strikes and brush fires in Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
Friday's severe weather left a trail of impacts across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County. Video sent to the WPTV newsroom from Sebastian showed a large waterspout passing over the Indian River Lagoon Friday afternoon. In Port St. Lucie, WPTV weather spotters captured video of heavy rain moving through the area.

 Merry Moore O'Rourke said her rain gauge caught over 3 inches. Moore O'Rourke described the sudden change in conditions, saying it got black, the wind started raging and the sky lit up like she had not seen.

 Severe weather stretched to Okeechobee County, where fire rescue crews airlifted a man to the hospital after he was struck by lightning. Port St. Lucie also saw significant lightning activity. Lucie County Fire District said crews contained a brush fire near the 1900 block of Castinet Lane after reports that a lightning strike ignited vegetation in a nearby lot.

 At the 900 block of Bellevue Avenue, fire crews responded to an evening house fire. Lucie County Fire District said it cannot confirm the cause, as the fire marshal's office still needs to investigate. Moore O'Rourke said the storms were radical and a little scary.
